lessons.title: Key Takeaways and Where to Go Next

children.text: Lesson 1 opened with a Mumbai prop trader holding a hedged position through the March 2020 crash, indifferent to which way the market went. Twenty-eight lessons later, you now know exactly what has to be true, statistically, economically, and operationally, for a bet like that to actually make sense, rather than just sound sophisticated. This final lesson pulls the whole course together and points to what comes next.

body.text: Statistical arbitrage is a market-neutral bet on a tested, real relationship converging, built from a regression-based hedge ratio and a formally confirmed, cointegrated spread, never from correlation, a good story, or an impressive-looking backtest taken at face value.

children.text: The Arc of This Course, in Seven Lines

cells: A market-neutral bet on a relationship converging, not a directional bet on the market
Correlate returns, not prices; build the spread with a regression-based hedge ratio, not a naive ratio; standardize it into a z-score
Correlation and cointegration are different properties; only a formally tested, stationary spread is actually tradeable
Screen with economics and liquidity before statistics; fix entry, exit, and stop-loss rules in advance; size positions by the hedge ratio, not equal rupee value
A hedge ratio estimated once goes stale; a filter that updates continuously avoids both freezing and jumping
6. Risk, Costs, and Why Backtests Lie
Transaction costs, look-ahead bias, and survivorship bias can each turn an apparently great strategy into a mediocre or fictional one
A pair is one instance of a broader factor; combining several factors, cleaned of overlap, builds a more diversified sleeve

children.text: The Single Most Important Habit This Course Tried to Build

Underneath every specific technique, correlation, cointegration, the z-score, the Kalman filter, orthogonalization, this course kept returning to one habit: never trust a single number without asking how reliably it was estimated and whether a real economic story supports it. A high correlation wasn't proof of a tradeable pair. An extreme z-score wasn't automatically a signal to trade. A passed cointegration test wasn't a guarantee the relationship survives a merger, a new competitor, or a regulatory shift. A great-looking backtest wasn't proof of a great strategy, until look-ahead bias and survivorship bias had genuinely been ruled out. That single habit, treating every number as a claim to interrogate rather than an answer to accept, matters more than any individual formula in this course.

This course covered cointegration testing, the Kalman filter, and factor orthogonalization at real depth, not as afterthoughts. The natural next step, Advanced Statistical Arbitrage: Multi-Factor Approaches, builds on exactly this foundation and goes further into territory this course deliberately left aside: testing whether an entire basket of stocks, not just a pair, shares a genuine long-run equilibrium using the Johansen test, and more rigorous, optimization-based ways to combine multiple factors into a single book, rather than the equal-weighted average this course used to keep things tractable.

Beyond that specific course, the most useful next steps are practical, not theoretical: get comfortable pulling and cleaning real historical data yourself, practice the walk-forward, honest backtesting discipline from Chapter 6 on a handful of real candidate pairs, and paper trade, or trade a small position size, before scaling up any real capital, exactly the caution Chapter 6 and Lesson 24 both argued for.

body.title: Your Next 30 Days
steps: Pick one real sector and run Lesson 13's screening funnel by hand on 5 to 10 candidate pairs
Pull at least a year of real historical data and run the correlation, hedge ratio, and cointegration steps from Chapters 2 and 3 honestly
Write down your entry, exit, and stop-loss rules from Lesson 14 before looking at a single day of results
Backtest with walk-forward estimation and check for survivorship bias in your own data source, not just in theory
Paper trade, or trade a small position size, before deploying your full intended capital

body.title: What was this course's real point?
body.question: If you had to summarize this course's single biggest lesson in one sentence, which of the following comes closest?
options: Any two correlated stocks make a good pairs trade

Every number in this pipeline, correlation, a z-score, a cointegration test, a backtest, is a claim that needs to be checked for how reliably it was estimated and whether it's economically sound, not an answer to accept at face value
Statistical arbitrage guarantees consistent profits if the math is done correctly
The Kalman filter alone is sufficient for a profitable strategy
body.explanation: This course repeatedly showed the same pattern in different forms, correlation without cointegration, a small-sample z-score, a stale hedge ratio, a backtest with look-ahead or survivorship bias, all producing numbers that looked convincing and were not automatically trustworthy. That habit of interrogation, not any single formula, is the course's real takeaway.

children.text: Statistical arbitrage is not a shortcut to easy, guaranteed returns, and nothing in this course should be read that way. It is a genuinely rigorous discipline: real statistics, real market microstructure, real regulatory and cost constraints, and, underneath all of it, real judgment about when a number deserves your trust and when it doesn't. If this course did its job, you now know exactly what work that judgment actually requires, and you are considerably better equipped to do it honestly than when Lesson 1 began.

points: Statistical arbitrage is a market-neutral bet on a tested relationship converging, built from a regression-based hedge ratio and a formally tested, cointegrated spread, not from correlation or a good story alone.
A tradeable signal needs an explicit, pre-decided entry, exit, and stop-loss rule, and a position sized by the actual hedge ratio, not by equal rupee value on each leg.
Relationships drift. A hedge ratio estimated once goes stale; a Kalman filter that updates continuously avoids both freezing and the discrete jumps of periodic re-estimation.
A backtest is only as honest as its treatment of transaction costs, look-ahead bias, and survivorship bias, each of which can turn a mediocre or fictional strategy into an apparently great one.

A single pair is one instance of a broader factor. Combining several factors, cleaned of overlap through orthogonalization, builds a more diversified, more robust strategy than any one relationship can offer alone.

All prices, statistical outputs, backtests, and case studies used throughout are illustrative and constructed for teaching purposes unless explicitly noted as real, publicly documented events.
